passage: I'm Ganga. I sit two desks from Salma at the accounts office, and I've watched her do something I didn't know was possible. When Mohan said he was leaving early for physio, Salma said, just as easily, "I'm off at five too, therapy day." No drama. When Hemant pushed, "Therapy for what?", she smiled and said, "That's mine to keep, but it helps." I think it cost her something, though I can't be sure. Last month our new trainee, Varsha, cried in the washroom after a bad review. Salma didn't say "poor thing". She sat down beside her and said, "Rough day. Want some water? If it keeps feeling heavy, our company counsellor is good." Since then, two people have mentioned their own counselling at lunch as if it were a dentist visit. I don't know if Salma planned that. I just know the room feels different.

qa.q: What did Salma say when Hemant asked "Therapy for what?"
qa.a: That's mine to keep, but it helps.

qa.q: What does Ganga think about how Salma felt when speaking openly?
qa.a: Ganga thinks it may have cost Salma some nerve or discomfort, though Ganga can't be sure.

qa.q: Which choices in the washroom supported Varsha without pity?
qa.a: Salma sat beside her, called it a rough day, offered water and mentioned the company counsellor, without saying "poor thing".

qa.q: Why might Varsha remember Salma's response differently from a "poor thing"?
qa.a: A "poor thing" might have made Varsha feel pitied and small; Salma's calm, ordinary words let it feel like a normal rough day with help available.

grounding: It shows a young woman at work who speaks of therapy as plainly as physio, keeps details private, supports a trainee without pity, and makes it easier for others to talk.

passage:
Diwali, Saturday. At Masi's house, Leela's cousin Sudha barely touched the sweets and said, "I don't know what's wrong with me. I just can't feel anything lately." Leela almost mentioned her own year of therapy, then held back. Too many aunts nearby, and she wasn't ready to say it in a crowd.
The next Thursday. Leela took Sudha for a walk by the lake. "Two years ago I had a really dark stretch," she said. "I saw a psychologist for eight months, the same way I saw a physio after I broke my ankle. It helped." She didn't say "poor you". She asked, "Do you want the name of someone good?"
Three weeks later. A message from Sudha: "Went for my second session. Also told my roommate. She said she's been wanting to go too. Thanks for saying it out loud, Leela."

qa.q: Where did Leela take Sudha the next Thursday?
qa.a: For a walk by the lake.

qa.q: Why did Leela hold back at Masi's house?
qa.a: Too many aunts were nearby, and she felt uneasy and not ready to say it in a crowd.

qa.q: What choice did Leela make on the walk, and why did it work?
qa.a: She shared her own therapy plainly, like physio for an ankle, and offered a name instead of pity, which made help feel normal.

qa.q: How has Leela's openness reached Sudha's roommate?
qa.a: Hearing Sudha talk about it, the roommate admitted wanting to go too, so one honest talk made it easier for the next person.

grounding: It shows a young woman sharing her own therapy only when comfortable, treating it like physical care, supporting her cousin without pity, and the openness spreading.

passage: "Lokesh, you asked why I spoke up at the team meeting last year. Sit. For years I told no one about my depression. When I was twenty-four, I took two months off, and I said it was a back problem. Later, when I felt steady and ready, I decided to say it plainly. At the meeting I said, 'I had depression and took leave for treatment, like someone would for a surgery. I'm well now.' No drama. No details I didn't want to give. A week later, Rekha from accounts came to my desk. She said, 'I think I need help too.' I didn't pity her; I just gave her my doctor's number and walked with her to HR. That's why I spoke. So the next person has it easier." Irawati refilled her tea.

qa.q: What did Irawati say her leave was for at first?
qa.a: A back problem.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when deciding to speak openly?
qa.a: Irawati felt steady and ready, comfortable enough to share plainly without drama.

qa.q: What choices in Irawati's story made her openness helpful?
qa.a: Sharing only when comfortable, treating depression like a surgery or other physical illness, and supporting Rekha practically without pity.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt approaching Irawati's desk?
qa.a: Rekha may have felt nervous but hopeful, encouraged by Irawati's honesty to ask for help.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls sharing a personal mental health experience only when comfortable, treating it like physical health, and helping a colleague seek help without pity.

passage: The baraat was due in twenty minutes, the band was already deafening, and the whole family was rushing. Sudha, twenty-five, found her cousin Divyansh hiding by the generator, looking pale. "Bhaiya's wedding, and I can't stop feeling like I'm drowning," he muttered. "Work, sleep, everything." Sudha had to shout over the drums. She kept it short. "Last year I saw a counsellor for anxiety. It helped a lot. It's like going to a doctor for a bad knee." Divyansh stared. "You? I never knew." "I tell people when it helps. Not everyone." She didn't pat his head or look sorry for him. "Want her number? I'll send it now." He nodded. She sent it, then pulled him into the dancing.

qa.q: How long until the baraat was due?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How was Divyansh feeling by the generator?
qa.a: He was pale and overwhelmed, feeling like he was drowning in work and sleeplessness.

qa.q: What did Sudha do that shows speaking openly with care?
qa.a: She briefly shared her own counselling experience, compared it to a doctor for a bad knee, offered the number without pity and kept it natural.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel pulling Divyansh into the dancing?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and warm, glad he took the number and can still enjoy the wedding.

grounding: Shows a young adult sharing her own experience only as far as she's comfortable, treating mental health like physical health, and helping a cousin without pity despite a noisy wedding.

passage: On Ishita's first morning back at the Gurugram office after six weeks of medical leave for anxiety, most colleagues avoided her eyes or spoke in soft, pitying voices. Ira, twenty-six, walked over with two coffees. "Welcome back! How's your week looking?" She treated it the way she would if Ishita had come back from a leg operation: glad, practical, no drama. At lunch Ishita asked quietly, "Did people talk about me?" Ira said, "A few asked. I said you were on health leave and that's your business." Later Ishita asked how Ira stayed so calm. Ira smiled. "I see a therapist too. I don't tell everyone, but I'm comfortable telling you." Ishita's shoulders dropped for the first time that day.

qa.q: How long was Ishita on medical leave?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when colleagues avoided her eyes?
qa.a: She felt awkward and worried, wondering if people had talked about her.

qa.q: What did Ira do that made the return easier?
qa.a: She treated it like returning from physical illness, avoided pity, protected Ishita's privacy and shared her own experience when comfortable.

qa.q: How might Ira feel when Ishita's shoulders drop?
qa.a: Ira may feel glad and quietly pleased that her openness helped Ishita relax.

grounding: Shows a young adult who treats a colleague's mental health leave like physical health, supports without pity and shares her own experience only as she's comfortable.

passage:
"Pradeep, you've been off since Monday. Everything okay?" Rekha asked, pulling a chair up to his desk.
"Just... tired. Stressed. It's nothing."
"Okay. You don't have to tell me anything." She paused. "But I'll share something, since I'm comfortable with it. Last year I saw a psychiatrist for panic attacks. Same way I saw a physio for my knee."
Pradeep looked up. "You? You're the calmest person here."
"Now, yes. Treatment helped. That's all."
"I didn't know people here talked about that."
"Most don't. But I don't think it should be a secret, any more than a fever is."
"I think I might need to talk to someone," he said quietly.
"The company helpline is on the notice board. Want me to send you the number?"
"Yes. Thanks, Rekha."
"Anytime." She squeezed his shoulder, not with pity, just like a colleague, and went back to her desk.

qa.q: What did Rekha compare seeing a psychiatrist to?
qa.a: Seeing a physio for her knee.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when Rekha shared her story?
qa.a: He felt surprised and then relieved, seeing that even the calmest person had struggled, which made asking for help feel possible.

qa.q: What did Rekha get right in this conversation?
qa.a: She shared only because she was comfortable, treated mental health like physical health, offered a practical next step and supported him without pity.

qa.q: How might Rekha's openness affect others in the office?
qa.a: It may make it easier for the next person to ask for help, because one respectful conversation makes the topic less of a secret.

grounding: Rekha shares her own experience when comfortable, treats mental health like physical health and supports a colleague without pity, making it easier for him to seek help.
